PAGE CONTEXT. This is a notebook page with two unrelated notes. It sits between remarks on integral domains/Dedekind and Galois (previous page) and Desargues' theorem (next page). The first note is invariant-theoretic: the nullcone and the ideal of invariants, i.e. the circle of Hilbert's 'Ueber die vollen Invariantensysteme', Math. Ann. 42, 1893. The second note concerns finiteness for finite groups of linear substitutions with algebraic coefficients.

NOTE 1 (ideal generated by the invariants).
- Setting. Let V be the coefficient space of a system of forms, with polynomial ring S = C[V] in the coefficients, and a group G (classically SL_n) acting on it. Let J_1, J_2, ... be the homogeneous invariants of positive degree, generating the ideal I = (J_1, J_2, ...) of S.
- Nullcone. Setting all invariants equal to 0 defines an algebraic variety N = V(I). This is the 'Gebilde' of nullforms.
- Claim A. Every hypersurface ('Fläche') F = 0 containing N satisfies F ≡ 0 mod I. Hilbert stresses: not merely from a certain degree on.
- What claim A means. In modern terms it says I(N) = I, i.e. I is radical (and saturated). The parenthetical contrasts this with the weaker statement that the ideal and the full ideal of the variety agree in all sufficiently high degrees (same Hilbert function eventually, i.e. saturation).
- What is generally true. By the Nullstellensatz one only gets I(N) = sqrt(I): some power F^k lies in I. This is how Hilbert 1893 uses it.
- Restatement. The ideal I 'contains all surfaces through the Gebilde', i.e. I = I(N).
- Claim B. If d is the 'dimension' of the Gebilde, then the first d invariants are certainly algebraically independent. All further invariants are roots of monic equations x^m + c_1 x^{m-1} + ... + c_m = 0 whose coefficients c_i are polynomial ('ganze rationale') invariants.
- Modern form of claim B. There is a homogeneous system of parameters J_1, ..., J_d of the invariant ring R = S^G. The J_i are algebraically independent, and R is a finitely generated module over C[J_1, ..., J_d], so every invariant is integral over it.
- Meaning of d [my interpretation]. For this to be correct, d must be read as dim R = dim V//G. Equivalently, d is the codimension of N when the quotient map is equidimensional. It is not literally the dimension of N. Also, 'the first d' must mean suitably chosen invariants (Hilbert 1893 takes suitable combinations/powers), not literally the first d generators in a list.

NOTE 2 (finiteness for groups of linear substitutions).
- Step 1. Let G be a finite group of linear substitutions in n variables. Its coefficients may be taken algebraic. All entries lie in a number field K = Q(alpha) of degree r. Every entry is then a polynomial in a single primitive element alpha (primitive element theorem).
- Step 2 (restriction of scalars). Choose the Q-basis 1, alpha, ..., alpha^{r-1} of K, so K^n ≅ Q^{nr} as a Q-vector space. Each K-linear substitution in n variables becomes a Q-linear substitution in nr variables with rational coefficients.
- Concretely [my addition]. Replace each entry a(alpha) by the r×r rational matrix a(C), where C is the companion matrix of the minimal polynomial of alpha. This gives an injective group homomorphism GL_n(K) -> GL_{nr}(Q).
- Step 3. The image is a finite group of rational substitutions in nr variables. 'Of the latter kind there are only finitely many.' In modern terms: finite subgroups of GL_m(Q) have bounded order (Minkowski 1887) and fall into finitely many conjugacy classes (Jordan 1880 for GL_m(Z); a G-invariant lattice reduces Q to Z; cf. Jordan–Zassenhaus).
- Conclusion. For fixed n and fixed field degree r there are only finitely many such finite groups, up to isomorphism/conjugacy, and their orders are bounded. This is essentially the standard proof of bounded order for finite linear groups over a number field of bounded degree.
errors: Claim A (every hypersurface containing the nullcone already lies in the ideal generated by the invariants, 'not only from a certain degree on') asserts that the invariant ideal is radical. The Nullstellensatz only gives F^k ∈ (J_1, J_2, ...). Radicality is false in general: for Z/2 acting by x -> -x the invariant ideal is (x^2), the nullcone is {0}, and x vanishes there but x is not in (x^2). For reductive groups such as SL_n, reducedness of the nullcone is a delicate property that fails for some representations (cf. Kraft–Wallach). As a general statement it is unjustified/incorrect; at best it holds in special cases.

Claim B: 'the first d invariants' cannot be literal. One must choose suitable invariants (a homogeneous system of parameters, e.g. obtained by linear combinations of powers as in Hilbert 1893). Also d must be the dimension of the invariant ring, i.e. the codimension of the nullcone in the equidimensional case, not the dimension of the nullcone itself.

Note 2: the degree r of the coefficient field depends on the group and is not bounded in terms of n alone. For example, GL_1(C) contains cyclic groups of every order, needing Q(zeta_m) of degree phi(m). So the argument proves finiteness/boundedness only for fixed r (or bounded character field), not finiteness of all finite linear groups in n variables.

Note 2: the final step ('of the latter kind there are only finitely many') is asserted without proof. It is a nontrivial theorem: Minkowski's bound for finite subgroups of GL_m(Q)/GL_m(Z), plus Jordan's finiteness of conjugacy classes. The finiteness holds only up to isomorphism/conjugacy, not literally.

results.what: Invariant ideal versus ideal of the nullcone: the hypersurfaces through the nullcone are exactly those in the ideal generated by invariants (claimed without a degree restriction)
results.modern_name: Hilbert's nullcone / Hilbert ideal; Nullstellensatz gives I(N) = sqrt(I); the claimed radicality is reducedness of the nullcone
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert 1893 (nullcone, via Nullstellensatz); reducedness questions studied by Kostant 1963 (adjoint case), Kraft–Wallach 2000s

results.what: Invariant ring is integral over d algebraically independent invariants (all others satisfy monic equations with invariant coefficients)
results.modern_name: Homogeneous system of parameters; Noether normalization of the invariant ring (Hilbert's second finiteness proof)

results.what: Finite linear groups with coefficients in a number field of degree r embed (via restriction of scalars) into finite subgroups of GL_{nr}(Q), of which there are finitely many up to conjugacy; hence bounded order/finiteness
results.modern_name: Weil restriction / restriction of scalars combined with Minkowski's theorem and Jordan–Zassenhaus finiteness; cf. Schur's 1905 bound for finite linear groups with traces in a field of bounded degree
results.usually_credited_to: Minkowski 1887 (bounds for finite subgroups of GL_n(Z)/GL_n(Q)); Jordan 1880 (finitely many classes); Schur 1905 (number-field version)

deep.surprise_reason: Note 1 restates the content of Hilbert's own 1893 invariant theory (nullcone, integrality over a system of parameters), with an overstrong and generally false radicality claim. Note 2 is a short sketch of the restriction-of-scalars reduction to Minkowski's rational finiteness theorem, which Hilbert would have known from his friend Minkowski. It anticipates in outline the number-field form later made precise by Schur (1905), but the sketch is incomplete and overstated, so this is a minor notable detail only.

checkable.asserts: The binary quartic x^3*y (a nullform with a triple root, normalized as a x^4+4b x^3y+6c x^2y^2+4d xy^3+e y^4) has both basic invariants i and j equal to 0, i.e. it lies in the nullcone; expect [0, 0].
Counterexample to claim A for G=Z/2 acting by x->-x: x vanishes on the nullcone {0} but is not in the invariant ideal (x^2); the remainder is x, not 0.

checkable.asserts: Restriction of scalars: the rotation by 45 degrees with entries sqrt(2)/2 in Q(sqrt 2) becomes a 4x4 rational matrix (sqrt2 -> companion matrix of t^2-2) of exact order 8, so a finite group over a degree-2 field embeds in GL_4(Q).
The companion matrix of t^2-2 satisfies M^2=2I, so the map Q(sqrt2) -> Mat_2(Q) is a ring homomorphism (basis of the restriction-of-scalars step).
